paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Wooldridge took place in Richmond, Virginia, on the evening of January 10, 1888, when an armed crowd pursued and fired on Wooldridge, a Black man accused of cutting a white youth, Emmet Branzell, in the abdomen. Wooldridge was wounded with birdshot, and according to the Richmond Dispatch the crowd called for a "rope" before police took him to the station-house. He was later indicted for the cutting, and in June 1888 a Hustings Court jury found him insane.

Wooldridge, twenty-six, said he had worked on an oyster-boat until two weeks earlier. According to the Daily Times, he and Branzell, a boy not quite fourteen, had "some words and a difficulty" that afternoon, and the boy told his father. At about 4:30 p.m. the father, R. H. Branzell, spoke with Wooldridge on Seventeenth Street near the grain elevator, and during the exchange Wooldridge cut the boy in the abdomen with a knife.

Wooldridge fled over Church Hill toward the river with many people in pursuit, the boy's father among them. He hid, stripped of his clothes, under a wharf at Rocketts while police searched with lanterns for more than four hours. About 9 or 9:30 p.m. he broke from cover, almost naked, and ran toward the gas-works. According to the Dispatch, several shots were fired at him before a Black man checked his flight, and he found himself "surrounded by a great howling crowd armed with pistols, shotguns, and everything else that would kill or wound." The paper reported "a number of calls for 'rope'" from a crowd that believed the boy dead and wanted to hang him, but said the police were "too active and numerous" to allow it.

Police covered him with a blanket lent by street-car men and took him to the First station-house. An examination that night found four birdshot wounds, three of them in the right arm, none serious. The coverage does not say who fired, and the boy's father said he neither saw nor heard any shooting. The Daily Times described the chase and capture but mentioned no shots or calls for a rope.

On January 11 the Police Court continued the case for ten days because the boy could not appear, and Wooldridge was committed to jail. Three days later the Dispatch reported him "quite sick" from exposure, though the jail physician thought he was pretending.

On February 11 a commission of lunacy found him "not deranged" and fit to stand trial for stabbing with intent to kill. He was sent to the grand jury on February 16 and indicted on March 5 for feloniously stabbing Branzell, who had nearly recovered. On June 6, 1888, a Hustings Court jury found Wooldridge insane, and he was remanded to jail to await transfer to the Central Lunatic Asylum.

Two Richmond white dailies, the Dispatch and the Daily Times, carried the episode in their local columns, with court items through June. The Dispatch headlined its January 11 story "VERY CRUEL CUTTING. A WHITE YOUTH ALMOST DISEMBOWELLED BY A NEGRO SAILOR," with the deck "Exciting Chase After the Latter and He is Shot and Caught Near the Gas-Works." It called Wooldridge "the shivering wretch," reported the calls for a rope without censure, and said the police "deserve great praise," while also printing "THE NEGRO'S ACCOUNT" beside the father's.

The Daily Times ran the story as "NEARLY A HOMICIDE. A Negro Stabs a White Man and Runs," said that the boy had struck first, and dwelt on the police hunt rather than the crowd. In later items the Dispatch called the cutting a "fiendish assault" and headlined the lunacy finding "Wooldridge Don't Get Off by Playing Lunatic," calling his behavior the "lunatic dodge."

The boy's father told the Dispatch that Wooldridge had earlier had Emmet down, and that when Emmet stepped up beside them Wooldridge "reached around and made two strikes at the boy." The Daily Times, by contrast, reported that the son "began to strke the negro with his fist" before the knife was drawn. Wooldridge said boys had called him "Injun" and thrown stones and that Emmet struck him first; the father doubted his son had interfered.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Wooldridge
bases: An armed crowd pursued a Black man accused of cutting a white youth, fired shots at him and called for 'rope' to hang him before police took him into custody (A1, A3).

A crowd described as 'great' and armed fired on Wooldridge and called for a rope on the belief that the boy he cut was dead, but he survived with birdshot wounds and was held by police, so this was an attempt, not a lynching (A1, A3).

The cutting, pursuit and police capture are reported independently by the Dispatch and the Daily Times, but the shots and calls for a rope, the mob element, appear only in the Dispatch; the Daily Times omits them without contradicting them (A1, A3, A4).

accounts.gist: After an earlier difficulty, the boy struck Wooldridge with his fist and was cut; police hunted and caught him after four hours; no shots or crowd threats mentioned.

framing.detail: The Dispatch headlined 'VERY CRUEL CUTTING ... BY A NEGRO SAILOR', called him a 'wretch', reported the rope calls without censure and praised the police, while printing his own account.
The Daily Times headlined 'NEARLY A HOMICIDE. A Negro Stabs a White Man and Runs', said the boy struck first, and centered the police hunt.
Dispatch follow-ups called it a 'fiendish assault' and mocked his 'lunatic dodge'.
